div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT A WARRINGTON FORGE.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT A WARRINGTON FORGE.

The circumstances attending the death of Fred. Edwards, a carter, which were briefly recorded in our last issue, formed the subject of an inquiry con- ducted by Mr. S. Brighouse, the coroner for South West Lancashire, at the Unicorn Inn, Winwick-st., Warrington, on Monday. Edwanls, who was a married man, and who was only twenty-four years old, was engaged by Mr. Filkington, contractor, and lived at 44 Leonard-et. Yesterday week he went to Bewsey Forge with • furry for a load of iron, and while assisting to put the material on the lorry lie was killed by some iron falling upon him. Mr. Thomas Morris, the general manager, appeared for the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, and Mr. Jenkins was present at the ingury in the interests of the relativea of the deceased..- The first witness called was the widow' Eliza Eilwards.who deposed that vile' last saw her husband alive on Friday morning. Ile was brought home dead on the evening of the same (lay. -Robert Low, warehouseman at Bew.y Forge, said that at about five o'clock on Friday night he was at the works when the accident happened. There was a lorry in the yard, which was being laden with iron hoops. The hoops were tied up in bundles, with three iron bands. Each bundle would weigh about half a hundred-weight. There were thirty-live bundles on the lorry when the accident happened. Deceased had taken a bundle to one side of the lorry, and had allowed it to slip over on to the ground. He got on the ground, picked the bundle up. and threw it on to the lurry. If the " skid " had been inn proper position the bundle would not- have rolled away. The "skids" were made of wood, from about a foot to eighteen inchou in length, which were fastened at their foundations by being placed between the Ade of the lorry and the iron. Ile was trying to put a "skid" in its place, and to do eu wits standing between his lurry and the stack of iron. The space between the lorry and the stack was about two feet six inches. As the deceased was trying to force the " skid " into ite proper place his jacket caught one of the bands of the stack behind him. Deceased pulled at his jacket to get it lon., and in doing no pulled over the bundle to which his jacket had caught, which brought down the other bundles with it. Decesenl was knocked against the lurry and was killed. In answer to Mr. Jenkins, witness said that ;here was no protection at the stack, but it had always stood in the same position. Lorries were loaded there regularly. Deceased would not have been on the side of the lorry nearest lie sleek, had it not been from the fact that the bundle had fallen off.—After another witness had given corro- borative evidence, the jury found that the deceased met his death by accident. They,bowever, recom- mended that, in order to preserve life in f uture,some protection be placed at the side of the stack of iron from which the bundle was dragged. -Mr. Morrie: Supposing the recommendation is carried out, and the men you have had before you to-day knock it down 84jBill : what most I do in that can'? -The Coroner Fin it up again.-- Mr. Morris It means extra labour for them. This is done not only in one, but in all the mills.- The Coroner: The recom- mendation does not impute any blame in the past. It only means that this unfortunate occurrence has shown a defect, which the jury think should be remedied—Mr. Morris: But I don't know bowls remedy it----Tile Coroner I know your inventive mind will put the matter right.—Mr. Morris I will carry the recommendation out to the utmost of my ability.- The Foreman: The jury are satisfied that Mr. Morris will do what is right.- -Mr. Morris : I am happy to tell you that the moment I found the poor man had left a widow and two children I appealed to our people to allow me to make her a grant of some few pounds, simply because the accident occurred at our works, although it is out of our jurisdiction.---The Coroner : Mr. Morris wishes to convey to the jury that his firm do not admit any legal liability. but out of kindness to the widow and children they made the grant—Mr. Jenkins: On behalf of the relatives and the widow I shall be very happy to take the company's kindness into consideration, end their thanks shall be conveyed in a proper manner. I have no wish to court legal proceedings.

' The Boulangists, discussing the consequences of their victory, believe that it will he followed by the immedi- ate fall of the Floquet Ministry, the dissolution of the Chamber, and the general election in March next. They also anticipate that General Boulanger's KlMss will have the effect of breaking up the Radical party and causing 40 deputies of the Left to join the General, who would then have 60 supporters in the present Chamber. rams, MONDAY M.Nl,..—General Boulanger left Cafe Durand at midnight, and drove home amid the cheers of the crowd. A Cabinet Council met at the Says', at eleven oelssch lass night, and lasted until one a.m. President Carnot will await the result of to-day's sitting of the Chamber before deciding upon the step to be taken. The Republican journals acknowledge the Republic has suffered a serious reverse, but add that Republica. should unite against ('asterism. The !tom langist and Monarchist organs declare that the Parlia- mentary Republh, stands condemned. No noteworthy incident in connection with General • Boulanger's return for l'aris had occurred up to Monday evening. Meetings of die Cabinet were held on Sunday night, and again yesterday morning, to consider the ! position of affairs. and M. Floquet, the Premier, boo, it ! ts stated, intimated his readiness to resign shonld the ! President or the Chamber deem such a course desirable ! in the interests of the Republic. The only reference to, General Boulanger in the Chamber of Deputies yesterday wan in the formal withdrawal of a question of which , notice had teen given eime time ago as to the measures ! contemplated by the Government with a view of stop- ping the progn,s of Boulangisni. The Chamber after- ! wards proceeded to discuss in a quiet way a bill for the ' improvement of the military ports. General Boulanger, in the COUTSP of an interview, has expressed his intention to show the people that the Government are the party of disorder, while he repre- somts the cause of order. ARREST OF MR. O'BRIEN, M.P.-SCENES IN MANCHESTER.

Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., attended a meeting at the Huhu Town Hall on Tuesday evening of the con- stituents of Mr. Jacob Bright. Mr. O'Brien wos ten- bated last' week to a term of imprisonment of four months for an offence under the Crimes Act. A warrant has since been out for Ids apprehension. A. few minutes before eight o'clock, while Dr. Woodcock (the chairman) was still speaking, Mr. O'Brien entered the building, and wasgreeted with wild enthusiasm. At the close of the Chaimun's spsveh Mr. Bright addressed his constituents on the work of the session, and spoke i shortly on the subject of Home Rule. Mr. O'Brien followed n a speech of an hours duration. Ile pointed out that a political refugee of France or Russia or any other country found an inviolable unctuary on the soil of England, but an Irishman striving to unite and knit together the hearts of the people of England and Ireland could be arrested iu the very heart of a free land. The offence for which he had just been sentenced to four months' imprisonment was that of uttering words which would be endersod by the majority of Englishmen. Mr. O'Brien spoke of the eir- cumstanres conneetol with his trial. Before the trial commenced the people were cruelly bludgtoned by the police, and 'those who at the peril of their lives entered the court were afterwards hustled and bludgomed out- doors because 51117 laughed at the name of the Crown solicitor. It was then that he declined to take part in the proceedings of a Star Chamber, made his escape through two hundred armed Men, and finally came to say a last word before his imprison- ment in the city represented by Mr. Balfour. Mr. O'Brien asserted that the Irish were conquering and not being conquered by the (iovernment, and at the close of an eloquent speech expressed his belief that the reign of taiercion would end with the next general elec- tion. WI ifs the meeting was in progress, a luge body of police tmder the command of the Chief Constable, was drafted in front and in the precincts of the building, and a vast crowd of people asumbled in the streets. As Mr. O'Brien was leaving the hall he was arrested On warrant, and, escorted by the police, was taken tattle Town Hall. The streets for the entire distance were filled with people, and the journey was in the nature of a triumphal pna-es- sion. At the Town Hall, Mr. O'Brien and Ins escort were received by the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Batty). In the Chief Constable's room, Mr. O'Brien was allowed to con-1 verse with the friends who had accompanied him. Mr. Leake, Mr. Ashcroft, and Mr. Ilrady availed themselves of the opportunity. Subsequently Mr. O'Brien pro- ceeded to the Mayor's private apartments, where he was to pass the night. The last visitor who occupied these rooms, we believe, was Prince Albert Victor. The Mayor stayed in the Town Hall all the night, and a strong force of police also rernainsal on duty in and around the building! JOURNEY TO IRELAND.

...--.—. On Wislnesday, Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., started on his journey b. prison. Contrary to expectation, he was not taken to the City Police Court. By special arrangement the half-past nine o'clock express from Exchange Station to Chester was stopped at Onlsal Lane, and Mr. O'Brien, driving there with the Chief Constable of the city, got into the train almost unobserv.d. The hon. member, W 1,., was placed in a first-class • compartment, was troubled no little 118 possible by the detectives who accom- panied him. At Chester, and again at llolyhnul, he had eonlial greetings from Home Rule and other friends who were eager to grasp his hand, and express both sympathy and admiration for him in his struggle. lie left Holyhead on the mail boat for Kings- lawn at half-past one o'clock. On his arrival there no organised demonstration was possible, still the people cheered him heartily. Ile svas conduct.' to the train, and P was thought would go on to Dublin ; but at the town station he was n.moved to another train, and his friends at Wnstland-row waited in vain. He was driven to Kint,eibridge terminus and, after the Lord Mayor of Dublin had insisted upon seeing the warrant, entered j another train, and would proceed by Limerick unction to his destination—Clonmel goal. At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday morning, Martha Varley, a woman of respectable appearance, was charged on remand with having, on or about the '2(itli of last November, she being a bailee of a piano, converted it to her own use, and thereby stolen it. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution. and Mr. Bremner (Liverpool) watched the case on behalf of the Pawnbrokers' Association. Mr. Browne stated that the prisoner was the wife of James Varley, who was in custody on another charge, and the two for many years kept an out-door beer- house in Folley-iane. In November lag she agreed to purchase a second-hand piano from NI esrs. 41. andJ. Weaver, furniture dealers, Bridge-et., on the hire system. The piano VMS delivend on Lie of November. and on the following day Mr. Varley:Cgned an agroonent for the hire of the piano, which was to be paid for by instahnents. One of the clauses of the agreement stipulated that the piano should not he removed from the purchaser's premises without the written consent of the owner, and that Sirs. Varley should be hold to 1v) the bailee of the piano until the while of the porcha.' money loot been paid. On the day following Rile went to the Tower pawnshop in Bridge-0., and asked for an advance on the piano. On being asked for the receipt showing that o.lle had pureluced the piano she said that she had lost it, and alleged that she bought the instrumott at an auction sale in Manchester. Ultimately Mr. Raynor, the manager, advanced ten guineas, and Mrs. Varley signed a declaration to the effect that she was the alwne lute owner of the piano. Mr. Browne, for the proses'. thin, said that Mr. Price was a member of the linn of Fmnklestone. Price, & Sins, trading as the British Furnishing Company, and lived at Cheetham, Manche,- ter. In this c4lo' the piano was WOrth 36 guin.,as, raid was obtained the day after the other was obtained by Mrs. Varley. The instrument was to be pahl for by monthly instalments, and the agreement wee entered into at the Conniany's shop in Johtestreet. Warrington. Prisoner afterwards disposed of the instrument to a broker, and it W. SOH to a Mr. Pownall, of Penketh, for £l5. That had ben repaid to Mr. Pownall, who had handed over the piano to Mr. Prier. div.p: .STRUGGLE.

Mr. William O'Brien arrived at Clonmel at 2.15 on Thursday morning. A large crowd assembled, and all the approaches to the gaol were guarded by troops. Mr. O'Brien on a ear formed the centre of a procession to the goof, and Hussars role Lefore and after him, while infantry surrounded the vehicle. After Mr. O'Brien hat been brought into Clonmel Gaol he was requested to undress and don prison clothes. This he refused to do. Warders therefore stripped him. He resisted dsvperately. His heard wiLS also cut off in accordance with prison regulations. The prisoner so exhausted himself by hio struggles that he became quite prostrate, and a priest woo sent for. This report has caused the greatest excitement in town. MR. O'BRIEN'S ADVENT-IMES. . .

..... ..... _ A Cardiff verrespundent is infortnol on good authority that Mr. O'Brien before going to Manchester was residing in a roast town of tilamorganshire, not far from Cardiff. The hon. gentleman, after escaping from the Police Court at Carrick-on-Suir,visited several tow in Ireland, and left that country in a small fishing boat, designated by the fi.shermen :IS a •• collier." In this craft he arrived in the British Channel on Sunday, being favoured with a strong suitable wind. On Sunday evening he dined at the house of a well-known Nation-- list, and slept there. On Monday he was stated to have driven about openly with his friend, but as Isis identity was absolutely unknown, except to one or two persons, the fact remainol unnoticed. Ile left South Walm on Monday evening for the residence of a friend in the Midlands, his Intention being to address Mr. Balfour's constituents in Manchester. The foregoing information was conveyed in a letter to a friend in Cardiff from a gentleman with whom Me. O'Brien took up his abode in Lilamorganshire. 1

div.head: PARNELL COMMISSION.
div.p: THE PARNELL COMMISSION.

The Parnell Commission was resumed on Tuesday, when but little interest was inaniferited in the proceed- ings. Sir Henry James concluded the reading of speeches up to the end id 1880, culling particular attention to addrmses delivered by Messrs. Parnell, Dillon, and Biggar, the latter of whom was reported to have said, at Dungannon, that the course reornmended by O'Donovan Rosso was the only one open to Irish tenants. Sir Henry James next quoted from speeches delivered sines 1880, saying he only intended dealing with the more important OOPS. He then went on to mad a number of extrarts from United Ireland,'' and was thou employed when the court rose. On Wednesday, Sir Henry James completed the read- ing of the extracts from United Ireland," and then procetoed with the letters which were found at the house of Mr. Matt. Barrio. Two of these were from Mr. Parnell, one asking Mr. Harris to join in an appeal to Irishmen abroad on behalf of the Irish tenants : the other declining to interfere with the stoppage of hunting by the Land League. The third letter was written by Mr. John Dillon, remonstrating with Mr. Harris for hav- ing attacked Mr. Davit, Mr. Hanley, a land agent in Tipperary, was then examined, and stated that in tion- sequence of the agitation he had to obtain police protec- tion. In egos-examination by Sir Charles Russell, he i said he had a battering von, which was necessary in conansmence of houses being fortified.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. FERRI' titY 2. 1889.

Tan scene which was witnessed in Manchester, on Tuesday night, will drive a long nail into the coffin of Coercion. It is a pity that it cannot be repeated in every large town in Great Britain ; it would be the death-the sudden death -of the Salisbury-Balfour Administration. Mr. Wiiiirtu O'BRIEN seems fated to baffle and vanquish "brave Mr. Hsi-roue." It was a daring thing for the member for County Cork, on Thursday week, when the Court was being cleared, to say that he would ' clear ; but he did it. He disappeared as if by magic, notwithstanding the guard of two hundred anneal men. There was a "hue and cry" after him for nearly a week ; but Mr. O'BRIeR, unheeding it, traverses four counties in Ireland, crosses over to this country, and re-appears at Manchester to keep an engagement ii speak at a political demonstration. Can we wonder that thew who heard his eloquent tringue,and those who from the greatness of the crowd could not hear it, cheered rapturously at the thought that O'BRIRN had again beaten Balfour arid his myrmidons ? The English people are slow to rouse them- selves, lint when they are roused they do riot, as a rule, turn aside (roma tank until it is accomplished. They are now roused on this question of the Coer- cion of Ireland, and they will make short work of the Crimea Act, after the next election. It is bitter as gall to be reminded that, after all our boasts about England being the asylum of political out- casts, it is no asylum for an Irish patriot. Com- menting on this, Mr. O'BRIEN said: - When I promised my friend, your most estimable and esteemed representative. Mr. Bright, to come to Manchester, I little imagined that I w•uld have to come as an outlaw, with almost, I may say, a price up- on my head; but so it is. I uproar before you with I scarcely know how many warrants and prosecutions and sentences hanging over my head. And the meet extraordinary thing is that if I were apolitical refugee belonging to any other land under the sun except Ireland, I could claim to-night nn inviolable sanctuary on the soil of England. If I were a French en. Russian refugee, England would light to her last man before she would surrender me. - ' (Cheers.) But I am only an Irishman- -fa voice, "God bless you ;'• and great cheers).- striving with all my might and with all my heart to unite and to knit together the beans of theme two nations; and the extraordinary thing is that what the French- man can claim, what the Russian can claim, I can- not claim. (Cheers.)

And what is Mr. O'Brien's offence ? Nothing more than daring to uphold rights of free speech and I fair-play, which ought to be hold sacred in every civilised country. Mr. O'Brien has spoken outand the sting of his statement to the Government and ' to the Irish secretary lies in the truth of it.

What, he says, was She very grievance of the speech for which I was condemned for four months' imprisonment the other My? It was the following sentence: --"If you want to know bow to deal with land-grahhers, ask the Primrose dames. (Laughter.) A,,lr them how they deal with the Radical shopkeepers who are guilty of a tenderness for Mr. Gladstone. The Primrose dames do not go round boycotting them is the hearing of the police. They do it a thousand times more effectively. When they meet them in the Street they give them the cut direct: they leave them severely alone But instead of sending these high titled dames to the plank bed, Mr. Balfour makes pretty speeches to them, and he receives bouquets ot flowers from them." (Laughter.) I suppose I was innocent enough to say, "Well, I suppose we can also tread the Primrose path of boycotting."--- (Laughter.) And no we can Icheers)--but with this difference -that the Primrose path of boycotting in Ireland leads not to garlands and flowers or ladies smiles, but, it iPIOI.I to the plank bed and to the county goal. (Cries of "Shame.")

Granted, for the sake of argument, that the member for County Cork is unwise in advising, his countrymen to practise boycotting after tho fashion of the Dames of the Primrose League, is it not monstrous that he should be put in gaol for an expression of opinion? If all politicians are tube "nun in" for giving questionable advice, one half of the country will become *ler to the other half; it will be in England as it is in Ireland—a case of" chaos come again." The law which enables the police of Manchester to march Mr. °Tama through the streets as if he were a felon is con- demned by the fact that the prisoner is applauded aa a hero. It is a villainously bad law, for under it "brave Mr. II ti.vors " has power to impri- , son not only the man who makes the speech, but the publisher who prints it, the newsman who sells the paper which contains it, and the children who offer it ,in the street! It has been the Irish Secretary's boat that he in no respector of persons—that he ' a dministers the law Se he finds it. But pnhile Opinion has become too atrong for him in the matter of locking up newsmen, and newsboys. The law is broken every day in every town in Ire- land, end he dam not enforce it. Tho time is rapidly approaching when he will he unable to enforce it against such patriots as the member for County Cork. The Crimes Act is a monstrosity; it is a staM upon civilisation : it is a disgrace to Englishmen ; the brutal instrument of a brutal Party and England will not be herself, nor will she deaerve to be herself, until it is effaced from the statute book.

ITHE Fair Traders are in an unhappy plight; they make no now converts, and they aru being &fantod by their apostles. Lord SALISBURY will have nothing to do with Protection, and now Mr. Hexer CHAPLIN, MP., who has hitherto been its advocate, haw turned his back upon it. Ho is understood to be hmikering after a seat in ' the Cabinet, and it may be that he feels that, by recanting, his chance will lie improved. Whatever may he the cause, it is significant that he has recanted. Speaking on "The Agricultural Depres- sion : its Causes and the Remedy: in the Abing- ton Corn Exchange, on Monday afternoon, he maid :

General Boulanger's success in Paris is startling; but it is not to be inferred from it that the Republic is on its lust legs. He culls himself is Republican, and if he is an honest man his election will do good. If he is a conspirator, he will doubtless be found out before hecan do much harm. In his address of thanks he says —"A: national Republican party based on the probity of its officers and the sincerity of universal suffrage is henceforward established in the chamber, which has fought against it with unprecedented fury." "The probity of its officers " is a good phrase. Let the General take it to heart, and he will do the State some service.

An interesting story comes from Vienna. "A 'Times' telegram says a scene of great min,. incurred in the Hungarian Parliament on Monday afternoon, owing to the ditumvety that detectives had been planed in the strangers gallery hi watch persons who might make demonstrations. As soon as the presence of these men was observed, the Opposition members rose in fury scrambled over the benches, and thronged on ihe door of the house, shaking their fists and shouting 'Turn them Out: The detectives decamped. for they stood in danger of being lynched.' Well done, Hungary! Thorns nothing like making a doter- ' mined stand for free speech.

Many of them used to think that this might be accomplished by a return to Protection. (Cheers.) Well, lie noticed the cheers which accompanied that statement, and he was free to content that lie was not at all altogether at one time opposeil to the opinion himself -(lieer, hear)---and he was very far from saying that it was impossible that some of them perhaps might live to see some return to some description of that sys- tem (cheersl—but his own viewg, he confessed, ' on this aubject had been largely modified within a recent period by two considerations. One of them was the experience of foreign countries. Every- body knew that in France and Germany protective duties of a very heavy character had been resorted to for some years. Ile believed that at the present moment in France they had import duties both on cattle and on wheat, and the tame practice pre- , sailed also in Germany. In France he was speak- ing from memory, so he would not guarantee being . absolutely accurate—they had a duty on wheat of Ps.. a quarter, and in Germany at the present moment ! there was a duty of tiomething like 14s. ; but not- withstanding that, if he might rely on the informa- tion sent by some of their Consuls abroad, not only had the prices failed to rise, hut in some eaten they I had actually fallen. The ether consideration was thia--the ireposdbility of carrying anything of the !kind at the present time. !Mr. CHAPLIN is right ; it is impessible in these days to get a majority of the members of the House of Commons to run after a Will-o'-the- Wisp. Mn dora well to largely modify his views when he finds—what we have urged again and again—that the countrim that practise Protection , tax themselves to no purpose. And having !largely modified hia views, he ought to do all he can to persuade other people to abandon their errors. It is a debt he owes to the truth. Mr. CHAPLIN'a present remedy for agricultural depres- !sion is a reversion to a bimetallic system. Can it be that he has dropped one craze to take up with another, or is he in the right this time

It is suggestive that the President of the United States has signed a testimonial :ilium, wiltaining a Home Rule address, which is to be presented to Mr. Gladstone, after receiving the signatures of as many eminent Americans as possible. Referring to the people of Ireland, the address concludes:— "The American people are with you in their desire for justice and pews., and wish you and I your associates added strength and roused and renewed deterinination to hasten the dawning of happy days, which will bring a return of goodwill , and prosperity both to Ireland and England." It would he interesting to know how many "eminent Americana" would sign an address of encourage- ment to Mr. Balfour.

It appears that he had been staying with a friend at Penketh, anti on Saturday morning Wa.4 on no Way to catch the Limepool train, when he was suddenly taken unwell, lie was assisted to the nearest house, but died in a few hours, heart disease being the cause of death. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest at the Walton Arms, Walton Sms,rior, regarding the death of a man, name unknown, which was foams floating in the Bridgewater Canal, on th•i 26th inst.--Phoebe (Salton, a widow, living at Walton, said that on ! Satiirday, about 1.84 pm., she noticed a body !floating in the Bridgewater Canal, in the parish of 1 Walton. She drew the attention of a canal bout- ! man to the body:—Peter Shearn, saddler, Walton. i said he assisted in recovering the body. It WWI !afterwards handed over to the police. --Mr. James Willett, surgeon. Appleton, deposed that he had made an examination of the body, and found it to . be that ot a man lift. 9in. or Iffin, in height with ! dark brown hair, probably about 45 years of age. ! There were no marks of violence on the body, and the colonr of the skin indicated drowning. The 1 body was that of a well 'developed man, ! evidently a labourer. It was dressed in a pair of , tweed trousers, with a leather belt round the. waist. There were cuts upon the frontal bones, 1 which hall been made after death, and scratches on' the side, which were also post mortem. The body i had probably been in the water ten days. The jury , returned an open verdict.

FATHER NUGENT AT WIDNES..

lln aid of the funds of the schools in ST. Patrick's parish, Seat Bank, the Rev. Father Nugent, the great temperance and social reformer, of Liverpool, delivered a lecture in Widnes Drill Hall, on Wednes- day evening. The building was crowded toita utmost capacity with an audience which evinced a deep interest in the proceedings. The chair Was OCCUied , by Mr. J. Morrison, who was supported by the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, Father Chapman (priest of the parish), Father Clarke, Fattier Brennan, and Father Byrne (Flint) ; Mr. Fitzpatrick (Secretary of the League of the Cross,Liverirol) ; Dr. O'Keeffe. Dr. McDonnell, Dr. McCambridge, Messrs. D. Forster, T. Smith, J. Fox, &c. In opening the pro. eeedings the chairman referred to the position Cat holies hail taken in regard to education, and said in Widnes the priests bad ever been foremost in promoting Mum- tion for the people, and the txtablislunent of dn.:tarok in West Bank District was another evidence tif their energy in this matter. t Applansc.)—Father Nugent, who was greeted with a most enthusiastic ovation, said he was not. aware that he had come them on behalf of education, hit understood from Father Chapman that he had to deliver a temperance lettere. If all the men in that room would only heroine tt,trotallers, anti would give for the purpose of education one fourth of what they usually spent with the publican. they WOlllll have the finest collection on behalf of education ever (mule in Widnes. (Applause.) The lectuntr then dealt in very eloquent language with the temperance question. and appealed to those pntsent to diseard the habit which was the cause of itt 1111 l eh want and niisery throughout the country.—Father Byrne delivered a SOIII stirring speech on the same subject, (mil afterward, Dr. O'Keeffe moved and Mr. Fin seconded a vote of thanks to Father Nugent for his presence and speech, both gentle- men referring to the heroic labours of the rev. gentle- man, fir the moral tind social elevation of the people. The !notion was carried by acclamation, and on the pro- position of than Finegan, Atconded hr Dr. McDonnell, a vote of thanks was t11..1/411Y1 to tint Chairman. Father Nugent sul.equently administensl the pledge to a large number of those present. During the evening, the 'children of the schools, who occupied the gallery behind I the platfo Inn, sang several part songs in a manner that called forth the warmest commendation. CATHOLIC BALL AT RUNCORN.

The annual Catholic ball took place in the Run- corn Public Mall on Wednesday evening. Instituted in recent years, this ball bids fair to become one of the chief and most pleasant social functions of the winter season, and although the company present on this occasion was not so numerous no last sear, , it woo Mal sufficiently large for the capacity of the ! hall, and the comfort of the dancers was not interfered with. The arrangements were on a most complete scale, and reflected high credit upon the bon. secretary, Mr. I'. Quinn, and those aswteiated with him. That youth should be frolicsome and gay, but when the frolic take. the form of interfering with railway points, and endangering valuable lives and property, for the fun of seeing a big sma.sh," it in high time that the curb was applied by the iron hand of the law, and the two youths who are now lodged in durance vile awaiting trial for committing such an outrage on the Ship Canal railway, should be made to learn very forcibly and very painfully that what in sport to them may be death to others; providing, of course, that the case is proved against them.

-71.17;it the that election of the Cheshire County Council has now become history, and the result, looked at politically, is encouraging to the party of progress in what is known as "Tory Cheshire." Latest calculations give the composition of the Council as 20 Liberals and 2$ Conservatives and one solitary Liberal Unionist. Should political bias enter into the labours of the new bodythere are not unlikely to be some exciting episodes in the selec- firm of Aldermen.

That several of the constituences were fought on "non-political " linen, Runcorn divisions amongst the number. Perhaps those who were elected as " Independents" may show themselves such by deed Bs well as title, and party distinctions will be of no avail. _

That we can all be wise after the event, and now the battle is over the remark generally heard with regard to the election in Runcorn North is Just as I expected." The larg, number of abstentions--one half of the electorate—in striking testimony to the lukewarm interest taken in the contest. All the name Major Haslehurst is entitled to the credit of his" glorious victory,' and he won the hearts of many by his genial presence, and ingenuous way of expressing his opinion. That in the South Division far more activity was displayed, and the poll was a heavy one. Both can- didates were of one political colour, and. in opposing each other, could not be said to have given up to piety what was meant for mankind. The rate- rayers hare made their choice, anti Mr. Speakman, elected by a substantial majority, has added one more tl the numerous public appointments he has held in connection with the town. That "The best of prophets of the future is the past." That in the Prodsham Division matters have beets made very lively indeed by the highly vigorous campaign the aucCeasful candidate has conducted, and that certain statements made by him are likely to form the subject of inquiry in the law courts. That the unopposed election of Mr. Snape to the Lancashire County Council is a matter for sincere congratulation amongst the Liberals of Widnes. A politician to whom the word " thorough " may be well applied, a social reformer of clear ideas, an authority on educational matters, and an eloquent speaker he in a man who may be expected to take an active and prominent position on the new body, and worthily represent the important town that centers upon him the dignity of County Councillor.

SUSPECTED MURDER IN NOCCOLS —Ayoung man named I Joplin is in custody at Lynn, Norfolk, on a charge of murder. He had been paying his addr.see, contrary to the wishes of her parents, to a young girl named Green, whose body was found in the Ouse on the 21st inst. Joplin was also found in the river at the same time, and he was, or pretended to be, ins semi-conscious state. He inquired for his "peer Louie," and informed the by- standers that "she jumped in" and he "jumped after her." The police have charged him with murdering the girl, and it is expected that the inquiry will beefs most marching character At King's Lynn on Wednesday evening a verdict of wilful murder was returned by a coroner's jury against Daniel Joplin, aged 29, in respect of the death of a pupil teacher named Franc. Louisa Green. Witnesss now spoketo Joplinhaving threatened the girl that if he "could not have hoe" he would kill her.

Mitchison was prominent with another goal run, but was final y tackled by Jolley in the home 25. The Warrington for- wards relieved by taking play back to centre, but the Wiganers retaliated by a combined rush to Warrington quarters, where the hone hum were of a free kick for offside play by the visitors, to which Williamson re- plied by a good kick to Daniels, which brought about half.time,the score reading—Wigan 1 minor ; Warrington nil. Mitchison re-started, and no return loeing niade, play Fettled in the home half. A grand movement, iu which Beard, Hayes and Creaghan were conspicuous, took play to the visitors' territory. J. Bate was next I to the front by a good tricky run, being brought down by Halliwell close to the hoe. By good forward play I and the aid of a free kick, the visitors carried play to midfield. From a scrimmage J. Bate passed to Moiher, who transferred to, Daniels, the latter getting away with a good run, and jost when about to drop over the line mar the corner flag was carried into touch by Halliwell. Jolley tried a but failed. A goal rush by the visitiors was checked by Daniels kicking into touch. The visitors made another incursion to the home line, forcing Jolley to concede a minor. The latter player's drop out was returned by Halliwell. Bibby secured and made a good run across the field, Williamson bringing him down. Play was of a fluctuating character, for some thee, the ball Gavel- ling in turns to both ends, finally resting in midfield, where the home team obtained a free kick, to which Mitchison replied to Jolley, who put in a huge punt to Halliwell, and the Latter failing to get in his kick, play tasted close to the line. Speakman stopped a rush by picking up and kicking to IVilliamson, who was tackled by Daniels before he could part with the oval. Shortly afterwards, however, Speakman secured, and by a ' dodgy run grounded the ball over the line, but the point was disallowed and a five yarfft scrimmage ' ordered, much to the disgust of spectators and players. Warburton subsequently got over, but this point also ' was disallowed. Lloyd, Donoghue, Dillon, and Warliur- . ton by a good dribble took play front the home 25 to ' centre, Freeman saving. From the ensuing scrimmage Beard, Bate, and Creaghan carried play to the visitors' ; quarters, where Bibby secured and made a nice run, ; ' being tarkled by Halliwell. The visitors relieved to ' centre, where Jolley got hold and put in a tremendous ; kick to Halliwell, who was forced to concede a minor. CIIESHIIik: COUNTY COUNCIL.

The elections of members for the Cheshire County Council took place on Tuesday. As a result of the contests the Council will be composed of 28 Con- servatives, 29 Liberals, and one Liberal Unionist. Owing to the extraordinary closeness of the voting, it is expected that a compromise will ho effected over the election of aldermen. Lord Egerton, who disposed of Mr. llough, his Liberal tenant farmer opponent, will be the now chairman of the council. Only one clergyman stood (the vicar of Sandbach), and he was defeated by the narrow majority of two votes by his Liberal opponents. Below wo give do- tailed accounts of the contests in various ,local 'divisions.
PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL.

On Monday evening a public tea meeting was held in connection with the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, begh-et., Warrington, the arrange- ments for which had been carried out by the married men. There were about 451 persona present at the tea, the tables being presided over by Messrs. Whitley, Bird, Cotton, T. Crampton, T. Shaw. Taylor, Higginson, Titchett, Podmore, and Williams, The subsequent proceedings were presided over by the Rev. W. Graham, who expressed his pleasure at seeing so many present. Ile could assure them that they were very vrticome, and he should be all the better pleased if he could by anything he might say enlist their sympathy for the object for which that meeting had been got. up. Those who were con- nected with Sunday Schools, and had to do with the training of the young, would know how necessary it was for the efficient training of young people to have separate and dietinct class-rooms. The want of that separate aceommodation was one of the draw- backs in connection with that school, and to his mind it was an exceedingly serious one. When first he came to Warrington beset before the teachers the very great need there Wlno for the construction of class-room accommodation, in order that the work of the school might be more efficiently conducted. It, laid down a plan by which he thought the school might he improved, and a large share of class- room accommodation provided, and that scheme he believed, the trustees were agreed on. The plan simply was to erect an upper school-room, and to divide the present one into class-rooms. By that means they would secure a very much enlarged school, and very much more convenient accommoda- tion. There were few people with whom he came in contact but had considerable sympathy with Sunday schools and their work, but it sometimes happened that they were not exactly so lavish with their sympathy as with their expression of it. He asked them to let their sympathy be material, for the question before them was simply one of ways and means. Ile was not endeavouring to SW that they were very poor people. He had a considerable faith in organization, and he believed that by wise organisation those connected with that place of worship could accomplish a very important result, even in financial matters. It only needed a willing spirit and a wise organization to no utilise the forces that they possessed as to bring about a very large help tor the scheme of alteration that they had designed. Ile believed that when they saw the necessity of the change they would be prepared to their utmost, not only by soliciting help from others, but by helping themselves. A miscellaneous pro- gramme was then gone through, the following ladies and gentlemen contributing :—Misses Fieldhouse, Williams, and Jones ; and Messrs. Fieldhouse, F. Williams, W. :Massey, C. Furness, A. Graham, John Jones, J. Philips, Bridge, W. S. Titchett, and James Shaw.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.

The return match between' the above clubs took place on Saturday at Wigan before 5,000 spectators. The first contest, it will be remembered, resulted in a victory for the representatives of the colliery town, although the Warringtonians had not their best team at play. On the present occasion the Lancashire County demanded theservices of players from each club, so that the teams now met on equal terms. Great interest was centred in the match, fully 2,000 journeying from Warrington. A slow driszling rain fell during the proceedings. At 3.20 Frank Turner started operation.s against a strong wind, Baldwin placing the oval in touch at the half nov flag. The first to show up R. Ashton, who executoil a neat dribble, until Slevin barred his progress with a smart save. Barnes and Slavin exchanged kicks, tho latter scoring a minor by a long punt. Frank Turner dropped out, and after some desultory play a forward rush by the home team reached the Warrington quarter flag. Barnes patina grand dribble' and Nevins gained ground by a useful kick into touch at the Wigan quarter flag. From a pack Halton got away, but Evans, picking up in grand style, punted into Ouch at the half way flag. Aided by the elements, the Wigan represen- tatives reached the visitors' line once more, and after Pilkington had responded to a dribble by Ftandles. But- tough got in a strong run, being grassed near the line. a minor following to the credit of the home team. Neutral ground was once more the scene of operations, and from a stiff scrimmage Antrobus and Speakman executed some neat transfers until Nevins raised the hopes of the Warrington supporters by a sterling run and kick. Give- and-take play followed, each side in turn having the best silt. Speakman came in for notice with a smart save, and Massey making his mark obliged with a judicious kick into touch at neutral ground. Free kicks to Wigan followed in quick succession, but the visiting defence was not to be tampered with. Sleyin endea- voured to force an opening, but Barnes, ever on the alert, secured his more burly opponent with commendable pluck. Now the Warringtonians went away with a combined rush, and reached the Wigan twenty-five, Wardle stopping their career. Baldwin responded, but pretty exchanos by Barnes, Antrobus, and Fair Turner relieved the wearied forward play, and exchange kicks by Slevin, Antrobus and Massey ended with advantage to the Warringtonians. The visitors were now playing a strong game, and the Wigan goal was in jeopardy. Antrobus and Barnes shone forth with grand work, and a tall kick bysliarnea waft only feebly replied to by Baldwin. A good dribble by Nevins and Povey ought to have ended in something tangible, but what chance there seemed to be of scoring was lost when Baldwin raced up and planted the oval in touch at the quarter flag. Nothing, daunted the War- ringtonianS played up with renewed vigour, and from some loose play Unsworth rushed the holt to the line, and when in the act of grounding lost possession, and Wigan luckily cleared. This piece of hard luck was discourag- ing to the visitors, and Wigan once more reached their opponents' flag. Another minor folloViSi to the home team,and although Fair Turner came in for notice Its tangible point could be scored. Barnes made his mark, but Frank Turner could do nothing with the place, and half-time NVB4 called with the score—Wigan, 0-0-3; War- rington, 0-0-0. With no tangible p.int scored against the Warringtonians, their chances of wiping out the defeat of the first match this season presented a most favourable appearance. However, nobody was prepared for the poor exhibition that was put forth, and the large assemblage was sorely disappointed at the play, it being chiefly confined to the forwards. Slevin restarted, the ball gravitating into touch at theWarringtonquarter flag. Here thegame was contested for fully ten misuses, and no many line-outs and scrimmages were indulged in that the game became most tiresome. Eventually Barnes relieved the monotony, for a tall kick by the Warrington centre was placed beyond the mark of Pilkington, who only ran the oral into touch just in the nick of time. A movement by the Warrington van presented a favour- able aspect, but all tons purpose, the coveted point was not to be had. Massey, Slevin, and Littlewood each in turn became prominent, but Unsworth ought certainly to have got in, but luck was against the" wire-pullers." Frank Turner was next to the fore, but his pass was intercepted, and another chance was lost. Pilkington had his kick charged down, but saved by running the ball hack which infringement of the rule ordered a pack on the line. From here Wigan relieved, and Barnes stopped a rush in clever style. Jolley now exhibited rare pluck by a capital save' but was tackled with the oval in his possession. A kick by Baldwin over his forwards was taken by Speakman, but the Wigan front rank tackled the visiting half before he had been allowed five yards. An appeal was made but all to no purpose, and the Wigan team taking advantage of the slight disorganisa. i tics that existed n the visitors' ranks rushed the leather over the line, and Brayshay grounded. The last. named, however, was fully six yards offside when he , pounded, baton appeal the verdict was against War- rington, the Warringtonians not charging the kick at , goal. Many timea it was thought that the game would not be played out owing to the partiality of the referee, and the visitors contented themselves by keeping the Wigan team at bay, and finally the verdict read—Wigan 0-1.3; Warrington, 0-0-0. Taken on tho whole, a poorer exhibition has not beon shown by either tram during the whole of their previous encounters. During the first half the Warringtonians played a good defensive game, and it was owing to their ill-luck in the second half that we must attribute the defeat. Barnes was the shining light of the visiting ' backs, indeed he has not been seen to greater advantage this season. His kicking and tackling of Slevin were ! accurately measured, and during the whole of the match he showed a consistency that calls forth great praise. Antrobus, Nevins, and Posey are deserving of notice. Teams :—Warrington : Evans, back ; Jolley, Barnes, ; and Massey, three-quarter backs ; Speakman and Ant], bus, half backs ; Ashton' ' Fair Turner Bandies, Little. wood, Nevins, Unsworth, Holmes, and Poyey forwards. Wigan Pilkington, hock ; Hall, Kevin and Baldwin, ' three-quarter hacks; Wardle. and Hallwell. half backs ; Dempsey, Lowe, Halton, Hatton, Telford, Bray-slow. ; Swift. Bibby, and Bullough. Referee, Mr. E. Beswick, ; Swinton F. C.

The division was divided into four sub-districts, via. (1), Daresbury, which comprised the townships of ' Acton Grange, Danwbury, Kekewick, Moore, and Newton-by-Hanel:airy ; pulling place, Daresbury Semi°. House. (2) Dutton, which comprised Anton-by-Sutton with Middleton Grange, Aston Grange, Rartington. Dutton and ; polling booth. The iChurch School, Dutton. (3) Halton, comprising Halton, Norton, Stockhaim, and Sutton ;polling booth, The (arts' Parochial School, Halton. (4) Clifton and Weston ; polling booth, National School, Weston. Mr. W. FL Brook was deputy-returning officer. At Daresbury the presiding officer was Mr. Spencer Wellhead, solicitor, Warrington ; and the poll clerk, Mr. H. S. Wellhead ; while the personation agents were respectively Mr. Thos. Houghton, jun., for Mr. Greenall, and Mr. John Hey- wood for Mr. Linaker, Mr. Harp being unrepresented. When the poll closed the ballet boxes wore taken to the Sessicas House, Deresbury, where the counting took place, and at a quarter-past ten o'clock the returning officer declared the result as fellows : I nap 369 Greenall 283 Lineker
APPLETON _DIV 'SION.

--.--., The candidates were Mr. J. Charlton Parr, Grappem ball Hey., Grappenball, and Mr. Joseph Knowles, farmer. Old Farm, Appleton-with-Hull. There were four polling statimig, one at rirappenhall, one at Great Budworth, one at Stockton Heath, and one at Whitley Superior. For No. 1 polling district the polling place was in the National School, Grappenhall. for electors entitled to vote for that part of the townArip of Latch- ford not within the municipal borough but within the ' parliamentary borough of Warrington and the township of Thelwall. For No. 2 district the polling place was in the National School, Great Budworth, for electors situate in the townships of Antrobus, Budworth, Great Crowley, and Seven Oaks. The polling place for No. 3 district was St. Thomas' School, Stockton Heath, for the town- ships of Appleton-with-Hull, Walton Inferior, and Walton Superior ; while the polling place for No. 4 district was , at the Board School, Whitley Superior, for oleetors for , the townships of Hattor., Stratton, Whitley Inferior and WhitlevSuperim. Thereare2ss personsenttled to vote in ' No. 1 district, 253 in No. 2,532 in No. 3, and 232 in No 4 district, the total number of voters in the division being, therefore, 1,305. At No.l polling district at Heap- penhall the presiding offiritr was Mr. B. L. Reynolds, of Chester, the poll clerk Mr. Jain. Hamilton, ((tappet.- hall, and the personation agent for Mr. Parr, Mr. John Wright Booth ; while for No. 2 district Mr. Thomas Garner, of Chester, was the presiding officer, and Mr. Philip Davies, also of Chmtor, poll clerk. For No. 3at Stockton Heath the presiding officer wag Mr. Wm. Hughes, Mr. Win. James, of Stockton Heath, the poll clerk, and Mr. Win. Speed officiated as personation agent for Mr. Parr. In the No. 4 polling district Mr. Josiah Longlands acted as presiding officer, and Mr. T. J. Jones, of Chester, an poll clerk. The votes were counted at Stockton Heath, where the result was made known. Parr Knowles

div.head: WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY. THE WORKINGMEN'S COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY. THE WORKINGMEN'S COMMITTEE.

The annual meeting of this Committee, which consists of representatives from the various works in the town, was held on Saturday afternoon, in the Mayor's Parlour at the Town Ilan, under the presidency of the Mayor (Alderman T. H. Sutton). There was a good attendance, Alderman Davies,' Major Litton, and Mr. Ziba Armitage, the honorary r secretary, being amongst those present.

10]1,111.13NTA'AVIES. At the commencement of the proceedings Mr. Armi- tage mid that 112 invitations had been sent out, and 44 replies had been received, nominating the following representatives to attend the one lag i—Al.srs. W. Fielder and W. T. Smithies (Armitage and Rigbys, Limited), John Griffiths and Charles Bunch (Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited), Thomas Burton (Monks, Hall, and Co., Limited), 'Thomas Wads- worth and John Berry (Rylands Bros. Mr. AIMITAGE also reported that the subscriptions for the past year, including the proceeds for the concert, totalled the suns of £430 ss. sid., being an increase of £62 over the proceeds of last year. There had, he said, been a considensble increase from several finns, which was very satisfactory. The Mayor also expressed the opinion that the result was very satisfactory.

It was then resolved: on'ibein:;;Sition of the MAYOR. seconded by Alderman DAVIES, that the representatives present, with power to add to their number, constitute this General Committee for the ensuing year. The following gentlemen were elected to serve on the Execu- tive Committee z—Meaner. John Roberts, W. A. Lloyd, fuseph Potter, W. Bidden, John Griffiths, Thos. Knight, Thomas Burton, J. Hartley, J. Taylor, U. Gill, J. H. Waring, Thomas Wadsworffi, S. Ross, C. Bunch, Henry Eyes, Wm. Crosskill, and George Legge.

Alderman Dvvics proposed that Mr. John Roberts he re-elected Chairman of the Executive Committee. He remarked that be knew of nothing in Warrington that had such a small beginning as the workingmen's fund , that had grown to such large dimensions. He was sorry to say that in most other places the working-men did not take so much interest in tile matter as in War- rington, but in Bury, and in one or two other towns they worked very actively, and their assistance wax very much appreciated. The assistance rendered to the Infirmary by the workingnten of Warrington was very highly appreciated, and there was scarcely a meet- ing of the Board of Management at which that help was not cordially recognised. He added, in proposing his I motion, that Mr. Roberts had been indefatigable in hisl exertions as Chairman of the Committee—Major Lirron seconded the proposition, which was supported by Mr. iitillITAOR and the MAYOR, and tarried with applause.— In reply, Mr. Rontotos, after thanking the meeting for re-electing him, mid that he knew of no infirmary within scores of miles of Warrington which was in As satisfac- tory and healthy condition as the Warrington Infirmary. Some two years ago or no there were a few complaints, but they had now disappeared, and be believed that everytlung was going on satisfactorily. Every patient who went there was well-attended to and courteously received. It would perhaps be interesting to know that the suhscriptions of the Workingmen's Committee were started in 1880. At the end of that year the subscriptions amounted n £lB5 9s. 30., and in 1888 the amount was £442 18s. 10d. Altogether £3,359 ss. 14d. had been sub- scribed in theperiod mentioned. He hoped that it would be found possible to still further increase the subscrip- tions.
It was then decided that the contributions for 1889 be handed in at the end of May and November.

Alderman DAviks, in a few complimentary remarks, proposed—" That the thanks of this meeting be given to Mr. Beamont, the venerable senior and chairman of the Board of Management of the Warrington Infirmary and Dispensary, on his completing the 6851 m year of his ,! connection with the institution, and earnestly prays ! that his long life may be still preserved to continue ! doing good to the town of Warrington." (Applause) The resolution was seconded by Mr. Joseph Port., I supported by Mr. John GRIFFITHS and the Mayon, and carried unanimously.

Mr. T. WADSWORTH said that he had been asked by a number of the workpeople at Messrs. Hylands, to pats question in regard to a letter that appeared in a War- rington paper a short time ago. There FM an Associa- tion in Warrington that provided its members with medicine and medical advice In rases of sickness— known as the medial assiciaton. The letter allegedthat there had been a meeting in a mom at the Infirmary, for the purpose of agreeing not LD bold consultations with the doctor of the Medical Association. There were at the works he represented a large number of men who con- tributed to the funds of the Infirmary,and who were also . members of the asmeiation in question, and they wished to know if any SOCII meeting had been held with the knowledge of the lhoard of Management.--Mr. John HOMO, said that he put the question at one of the hoard meetings, and received a reply that such a meet - , Mg had never taken plait —Mr. WADSWORTH mid that !he was pleased to hear that reply ;it would give great !satisfaction—The Mason Alto well that ends well.
The Preoident and liedic-irofice—r's of the Infirmary

were thanked for their services on the motion of Mr. Fietring,seconded by Mr.lintesermi.—Mr. %lila Armitage was re-appointed hon. secretary on the motion of Major I.arros, seconded by Mr. Honorer and supported by Alderman Dooms. and Mr. Armitage was thanked for his services during the past rear on the proposition of Mr. John ROBERTS,ReeOrIded by Mr. Cuossgim..—The pro- ceedings terrninattxl with the passing of a vote of thanks : to the Moron for presiding. •. LETTERS.
We have been requested by Mr. Ziba Armitage, the hon. secretary of the Workingmen's Committee, to pub- lish the following letters, which will he road with great interest

!"---I•Vorkingmen's Commit ee, 28th January, 1889. Bear Sir,—The annual meeting of representativm from the various works in town has been held this afternoon at the Town Ball, under the presidency of the Mayor, when, I am happy to inform you, the following resolution was heartily adopted, after being moved and seconded by delegates who were present • "flint the thanks of this meeting be given to Mr. Beaenont, the venerable and senior chairman lithe Board of Management of the War- rington Infirmary and Dispensary, on his completing the 68th year of his connection with that institution • and they earnestly pray that his long life may be still. pre- served to continue doing good to the old town of War- rington.- As general secretary of this Committee, I have the honour of sending this resolution, and with an expression of my personal regard, I am, sir, yours very sincerely, ...„„,

z,. AUMII,OB. Orford Hall. Warrington, January 29th. Dear Mr. Arinitage,—Thank you very much for your kind letter of the 26th and its enclosure, containing such a satisfactory proof of the value which you and the workingmen of Warringtan net upon the benefits of the Infirmary and Dispensary. !think the list of their sub- scriptions reflects the highest credit upon themselves, and I beg you to convey to them my wannest thanks for their kind expressions to myself. I remember with great pleasure the way in which the workinginen of Warrington came forward to provide the handsome por- trait of the InArinary's great benefactor, Mr. Hatton. At the time of toy early connection with the old Dispensary. (66 :ears ago, as ynu stated) we had great difficulty in getting subscriptions for its support. Now we live in happier times. I beg you to accept my acknowledge- ments of your own valuable services to the institution, and to reciprocate all the good wishes you express to me.—Belieue me, yours very truly,
WILLIAM BRAMONT.
, WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH,

From the " Year Book " of this Church, just issued, it appears that the membership now:stands at 306. In free-will offerings the slim of £621 15s. fli had been received between Ist 0ct.,1887, and 30th Sept., 1888. During 1888 the sum of £1,145 Iss. 4td was received as special collections. During the year 38 meetings of the Ladies' Dorcas and Working Society were held, and many gar- ments were given to people who were found to need them. Since the formation of the Catechumen Class in 1881 it had linen joined by 186 young people, and on New Yeats Sunday each of the then members, as is usual, received, sea gift from the church, a Bible bearing an appropriate inscription. From October to December last 126 members joined the Young People's Society, which superseded the Mutual Improvement Society, and the average atten- dance was about 80. The Rev. John Yonge is president of the Society, Mr. A. G. Wallington is treasurer, and Mr. It. Lowe secretary, and the Society also owes much to the constant attendance and encouragement of Messrs. Donlon and Wylie.

The annual tea tfi-e-etirTg;lt; cOn-n-e-cat'm with the Sun- day School took place on Monday and Tuesday week. The first meeting was for the adult members of the school, and it was very well attended. The tables were presided over by the teachers of the respective classes. After tea, while the room was being cleared, games were played in the class-rooms, and: the subsequent proceedings were presided over by the Rev. John Yonge. Lluring the even- ing prises were given for regular attendance and good conduct, the recipients numbering 116, being an increase of 20. The presentations were made by Mr. Brown, the superintendent. Songs were given by Miss E. Wallington Mr. A. Griffiths (encored), and Mr. W. Brown; a recita- tion was contributed by Mr. J. Evans; a pianoforte solo by Mr. IS. H. Payton ; a glee. "Johnny Schmoker," was given by Messrs. W. H. Wallington, G. Smith, Podmore, and W. Brown ; and Masters Place, A. and P. Longshaw, Podmore, and Sanders, rendered a dialogue, "No end of a pickle." The attractions also included a magic lantern entertainment, under the direction of Messrs.. Corney, T. Wallington, and W. H. .Wallington. On the I Tuesday evening there were about 200 of the infants present, and, after tea, there was an entertainment. It may be added that the school roll contains the names of 691 scholars, an increase of? upon last year. The aver- age attendances were as follow : morning 232, an increase of 5 upon last year; afternoon, 400 a decrease of 10. This is accounted for in the infant class, the other classes in the school having a better afternoon aver- age than last year. The class contributions to the Missionary Society were higher than in 1887, though lena money had been raised by means of missionary boxes. I During the year the service held in the school lathe I morning had been well atended, an average of 103 hav- ing been attained.

Similarly with other schools in the town, sickness has again reduced the average attendance, that in the upper school being 334, and in the infants 81. In October, 384 scholars were presented for examination. The accounts sheen that a satisfactory balance remains to be carried forward. Mr. A. Comey is the head- master.

This mission is coder the C11.4-igTof the Rev. John Davi., who suGasded the Rev. W. Parry, that gentle- man having accepted an appointment at Teasley Croon, St. Helens. There are 512 .holars on the books, 245 males, and 267 females ; the average attendance in the morning h. been 220, and in the afternoon 325, this attendance being in advance of last year. The accemo- dation provided by the school premises and chapel is very inadequate for the efficient instruction of so many children, an infant mom and several class-rooms being urgently required. There are 23 officers and teachers. 11 males, and 12 females. The superintendent for the year is Mr. T. R. Malkin ; assistant, Mr. J. Astley ; .cretary. Mr. G. Maybury, assistant, Mr. J. Ashton; harmoniumist, Mr. S. Walker. Early in December, the officers and teachers agreed to commence a service at 5-15, for one hour every Sunday evening, for the ragged children in this neighbourhood who do not go to any Sunday school, as they had reason to believe there were a large number. The first service was held on Sunday. January 6th, and though owing to the extra work at Christmas time, no organized effort could be , made to canvas the neighbourhood, 110 children of the poorer class attended.

MeMinnim appeared in support of an appeal against the assessment of his residence, Bewsey-road. The assissment was £BO gram, £l3B rateable, but as it was explained that at the expira- tion of a lease the rent had been lowered to £5O, the assessment was reduced to £5O gross, £42 10s. rateable. Tux CONSERVATIVE Cxce.—Mr. H. Collin appealed against the following assessments in connection with the Conservative Club :—Office £l5 gross, £l3 rateable; Assembly room £5O gross, £42 10s. rateable; house £l5 grass, £l3 rateable; bowling green £25 gross, £2l rateable. The ground of appeal was the fact that a reduction had been made in the rent paid to the Conservative Club Buildings Company.—The Chairman said the rental could be no criterion in a case like this. In this case it was like Satan occupying his own house. The Liberal Club vra.s just in the same position.—The Valuer mid he did not know at any reason for reducing the asses.srnent of these buildings.—Mr. Collin mid the only ground he appealed upon was the reduced rental.— The Clerk Can you show a depreciation.—The Chair- man mid that on the contrary property in the , position of the Conservative Club ought to be increasing n value.—The appeal was not allowed. Tax BRIDGEWATER CANAL.—'fho Clerk said thatthe 1 31aarliester Ship Canal Company were appealing against , the assessments over the whole length of the Bridgewater Canal. As there was only a comparatively short length of the canal in Warrington Union he had informed a representative of the Company's .licitors that that Committee would probablyhe willing to follow, without further litigation, the Insult of their appeal in some other Uniou niore deeply concerned. This seemed to be perfectly agreeable, and he (the Clerk) mastoid that the Company would certainly go to quarter sessions with one or other of the Unions if they did not get a remedy. Another reason why that Union should not spend a greet ainount of money on the matter was that the canal would almost entirely be taken out of their Union if the Cheshire County Council were determined to take the Chmhire townships. This arrangement of the Clerk was approved of by the Committee. VALUER'S REPORT.—Thd Valuer reported that since the last meeting be had made the following valuations ;—Mr. T. H. Thoruley,rt. This was all the business.

--117:dileie;•".(Wannitarros) v. Trtarro ilssent.—These teams played their return fixture on the ground of the latter, on Saturday. The borne club had got together very strong team, with the determination to wipe out their previous defeat, but in this they were again disappointed, as Wycliffe ultimately Cannot winners ' by a try mid four minors to two minors. Two thirties having been agreed upon, the home captain kicked off, and a good turn been made the Wyeliffites at once assumed an aggressive attitude. A series of scrimmages , were formed near the home line, where Webster got hold, and in a splendid shot at goal scored the first point, a minor. From the drop out tho visitors were Z once more found in the aseendancy, and a mull by the Thatto Heath back let in Chappell, who scored between the posts J. Knowles, however, failed to augument its value. Half time was shortly afterwards called, the visitors crossing over a try and two minors to the good. I the second half developed into an exhibition of strength. The) !stmt., team, seeing themselves outclassed, played a I mule, Rftme Iseith the intent of securing a major ' point, but were frustrated by L:2 fine defence of the I Wycliffe backs, Sampson at full back played a splendid game, being equally well supported by the remaintlig harks, of whom Webster was the pick, whilst the for- I wards exhibited their usual combination and dash. It is only fair to state that the visitors had several tries dis- allowed, the decision of the referee being anything lout satisfactory. The following was the Wycliffe team Full hark, W. Sampson ; throe-quarter backs, J. War- burton, A. Jones, and H. Webster ; half back, W. Knowles and G. Griffiths; forwards, W. Cotton (cap. , taint, E. Hackett, H Haves, W. Lowe, J. Knowles, J. Chappell, W. A. Cleave, Dainteth, and E. Booth. CIIRSIAIRE V. NURTHUMBERLAND.—TiIiS county fixture took place at Birkenhead Park, onSaturday. The weather was fine but cold, and there was a good attendance of spectators. The visitors kicked off against the wind, and Holden returned into e ouch. Cheshire then had the best of matters, and eventually Wolff ran well, kicking and following up no smartly that he collared Graham on his own 25. The ball was then kicked across the field, and Wainwright getting posscsaion, dropped a fine goal, although surrounded by his antagonists. Cheshire continued to assert their superiority. Monteath, and , Hughes being conspicuous with smelt play, but even- ) tually the Northumbrians broke away, and almost got over, Wainwright saving finely, bat from the subse- quent scrimmage Monteath came through finely, and passed to Hughes, who gave Wolff possession, and the Altrincham exponent got in a nice run before Ilubertaon arrested his progress. Cheshire then presented a bold front, and at length Wainwright secured the ball and effected a grand run in, but Wolff failed to improve the point. Half-time arrived without any further tangible point• being scored. On changing ends and resuming the vsitors had the wind in their favour, and quickly assumed an agg,reasive attitude. Drinkwater then canto , to the rescue. Evenly-contested play then followed, Wolff getting in some grand playand tackled Hubertsen grandly when a try looked imminent. Eventually, however, Wainwright secured an easy try, but Hughes was unsucceseful in his attempt at goal. After give-and take play, in which Wolff and Monteath showed up for the Custrians Wainwright scored a grand try, which limed). failed to improve upon. Northumberland then relieved the monotony and scored a minor, but Wainwright again got another try, after a really fine run. Wolff undertook the place, but failed, and Cheshire wets ultimately hailed the victors by one goal, four tries, and five minors to one minor. The visi- tors worked tho oval close to the home line, Mather affording temporary relief by kicking into touch. The home team obtained a free kick for a knock on, which took play to centre, J. TIMELY RESCUE OF A CHILD. (From The Raw 0e:do) The following Interesting facts regarding the timely rescue of a child have Just been brought to light, and are made public by the father of the little child, Mr. W. U. flaw, the well-known baker ; and grocer, of 2,3, Iligh-st., Redcar, We may add that the publishers of this paper, being familiar with the facts, are in a position to personally vouch , for the entire accuracy of the particulars given. lAs the incident is no doubt of decided importance to parenrs, we gladly become the medium of bringing it to the notice of the public i—" Some little time ago the jyoung daughter of Mr. Haw became the victim of an jacute bodily affliction of a rheumatic nature, which attacked the arms and legs of the child, so that these I became alarmingly swollen and painful. Notwithstand- ing the Steps which were taken to relieve the little sufferer,her case became so serious that she not only was j confined to her bed, but was unable to torn her body' from one side to the other. At this critical point, every- thing having hdled, Mr. Ilaw remembered having read j of a disoivery which possessed almost magical power to drive away pain. He procured a bottle, and -made an! application. To his agreeable surprise and satisfaction, the pain and swelling began to disappear immediately,in twelve hems the child could walk across the room, and when only three applications bad lx-en made the pain and swelling bad entirely left her, and she is now quite well. Mr. Haw very aptly remarked that a remedy I prosessing such wonderful power as St. Jacobs Oil, which is the article used on the child, should be made known by every legitimate mum, as by its use, no doubt, untold suffering would be avoided.'

SEAMEN'S WAMMA-The Glasgow shipowners Wednesday met and resolved to give the seamen 27 s. instead of 255. per week as at present. It is expected that the men will accept the concession. At Liverpool the strike con- tinues as before. In some cases increased wages are paid; in others they are infused.

div.head: "LAW AND ORDER"
div.p: "LAW AND ORDER"

tine of the signs of the times is the growing dis- like manifested to rendering obedience to laws which, rightly or wrongly, are considered bad ones. Society can hardly be in a healthy condition when any number of its members feel conscientiously compelled to set themselves up as the final stand- ards of appeal in matters of more than individual moment. It is really becoming a serious ethical question of the day whether men are bound to obey bad laws; a question removable by easy transition into the region of practical politics, Mas- i:lWO so individual law carried to its ultimateis the negation of all government --a system of anarchy and confusion. The point at which allegiance to State laws shall cease, and an unflinching fidelity to the Supreme law" above all the enactments of human codes- commences, is to be determined by each one for himself. This may appear to throw open wide the door to anarchy; but if the exist- ence and authority of the higher law of conscience be admitted, it necessarily follows that the indivi- dual. fur whom alone it has a voice, is a law unto himself. One voice alone he hears, and to hear in to obey though the heavens fall. Men born, cradled, reared amidst an environment of laws enshrined in the high sanction of antiquity feel, as a rule, little or no desire to rebel against such weighty authority. But then, have ever been cluisen spirits who, obedient to the light within them, have smitten hoary prejudice, broken the iron chains of custom, defied the laws of tyrants. and thus opened a new path for the coming generations. historically. obedience to conscience has always initiated great moral movements, and such movements are all powerful in deciding the destiny of nations. The champions of" law and order" in Ireland Mr. Balfour and his myrmidons --are to be con- gratulated on the service they are unwittingly ren- dering to the British democracy. The senseless anti inhumane manner in which the law in administered is not only discrediting in the eyes of the electors of this country, the Government sanctioning ouch uncalled for coercion, but is bringing about a reign of conscience in conflict with which Balfourism must inevitably bite the dust. It has been well said that had conscience the power, as it un- doubtedly has the authority, it would rule the world. But. unfortunately, the might of the world Y. too often been arrayed against right and justice for unto even hope that such will not again be the case in the &Helmet the Sister Isle. But there are hopeful signs, nevertheless. The Irish leaders are showing themselves free men. They cannot, they have no inclination to resist the armed forces of the Crown. But on the other hand they have no intention of yielding. Theirs is a "just cause con- secrated by centuries of suffering"; and now that the Britinh democracy, touched by a strange new feeling,hiss ranged itself on the side of the oppressed, the day cannot be far distant when the music of a peaceful and contented people shall again fill the graceful valleys of Old Ireland. Meanwhile the misgovernment of Ireland is still carried on. The arrest of Mr. O'Brien in Manchester and the sentencing of Mr. Sheehy M.P., to six months' imprisonment. both of which events occurred on Tuesday last,are sufficient to show that the struggle for liberty is proceeding apace. But the National sentiment of Ireland will never again be crushed beneath the tyrant's heel. The conflict fierce and long as it has, and will be, shall end in victory. When, in the name of "law and order," unrelenting tyranny rules, men may ever find a . guide and law-giver within them whose decisions ' are final and beyond appeal. And in this exaltation of conscience in Ireland, and the sanction given to such conduct by a growing public opinion, lie who will may trace a further real development of the British democracy a development which, when moved further along such lines as may be determined by Eternal Righteousness, will eventually usher in a new dawn of peace, equity, and liberty.

COUNCILLOR MONKS . AND THE SANITARY
UTTEE

Sir—Last Friday night, at a ineeting of the Town Council, there was a debate about the proposal of the Sanitary Committee to purcha. a Flrman's dryer and engine for £4OO. Whilst 1 was speaking, Councillor Monks interrupted and contradicted me. I think rudely, and said :—" You have been losing £4,000 or £5,000. You lost more than that last year.'

Mr. Monks when he said this, included the cost of col- lection which is quite a separate item, and man expense which must be ineumsl no matter what system is adopted for dealing with the refuse of the town after collection. Mr. Monks was, therefore, trying to mislead the Council and the ratepayers by including the cost of the collection in the expenses of working the depAts. Mr. Cliodey informs me that the expenses at Long- ford and the other depiits, for the quarter ending Decem- ber 315t,18138, were £550. illiS multiplied by four, gives £2,200 for the year. The interest and the Sinking Fund for Longford dew', is under £BOO a ymr, to that if we can make 10 tons of manure a week (and I believe we can if we have is. accident at Longford) worth £6 per ton, we have £3,000, and that will cover the whole of the Working Expenses and the interest and Sinking ! Fund at Longford depa. I deft Councillor Monks or anyone eLse tn quote any city or borough in the Enited Kingdom where the results are equal to ours, especially when we can do this work with- out beings nuimnee. That, after all, is the most diffi- cult thing to do. Rochdale is often quotisl. Take the results at Rochdale, and they are not nearly SO good as ours. besides the stench in the works at lioclidsle was something awful when I was there.

If w;:.had in Warrington our old ash midden system, the cost now would be £6,882 per year. Under our present system, the total cost, including collection, expenses of the depots, interest and Sinking Fund, is £6,483 per annum, no that, after paying all the rost of eollontion and expenses, we have £3,000 worth of manure to the good, and vet Councillor Monks rudely ; interrupted ine and said-4 You have been losing £4,000' or £.5.000..a yentrf:

Councillor Meeks was angry when we first adopted our present system, and did his utmost to make us use fire heat an they to at Rochdale. and I am afraid that be is not pkias.ed now when he finds we were right and he_was wrong.

My only object in writing lbw letter is to let the Rate- payers know the true facts of the matter, and to show that Alderman Burgese and the Sanitary Committee de- serve praise rather than Maine. I may add that the mist important result of our work, has been the reduction of the death rate from 32 to 22 in the thoukand. 'I his must be satisfactory to every reason- able man, even if we did not save one shilling in en- penses.—Yours truly,
