THE mcomEst ROAD IN TOWN.

Sir,—Allow me through the medium of your columns to Mil attention to the shocking state of Wilderspool Causeway. I have lived in Warrington along time now, but I never remember seeing a public thoroughfare kept in such a disgraceful condition, for on long a period, as the road I have mentioned. I verily believe it is to-day the muddiest road in the whole town. From Friday noon to the following Friday morn mud reigns supreme. Street sweeper:. are a eurieeity in this neigh- bourlood, and on the rare occasions upon which they do put inan appearancetheir labours arespeedily obliterated by the heavy traffic along the Causeway. This traffic has increased enormously during the past twelve months, cutting up the road to a fearful extent. and causing the mud to bespatter every thing and everybodyalong its route. Yet the old e.y-going ways co( clemoing the road are still r flowed, too tho annoyance and disgust of all who are conmellol to use if oltorough. fare. One day a couple of men will commence to scrape the read, an operation which lasts the greater part of a week, then the wavengers will have a turn with their brushes, and, finally, the accumulations will be slowly carted off . Why the sweeping machine does not go two or three times a week to the borough boundary I cannot makeout. Morning after morning I notice it sweeps the front of Councillor Taylor's door, and then ceases its work. Sow, why rant it continue past my neighbours' doors and my own? I have to pay rates as well as other people; but it seems I pay not for my own enjoyment but in order that some better-favoured residents may have privileges that are denied to me. Hut I've been splashed often enough, and I think it time the scavenging department had its attention drawn to its neglect of the Causeway. Every day this week it has been unfit for a decent person to sr.., anti at the moment I write lakes of mud, inches deep, mark the entire length of road. lane surprised at : the supineness oof tny neighbours in this matter, and I hope, now the ice is broken, they will second my efforts to bring about a better state of things.—Yours kc SILL

IS PORK INJURIOUS? Sir,—Twice a week, for hours at. stretch, I hear doleful, ear-piercing shrieks from porcine victims to the : slayer's knife As they protest to their latest breath against being deprived of the enjoyment of life. Never- theless their bodies are to be 64an next morning suspended heels uppermost to the beams of the now silent shambles, and, later on, they are carted away in loads an pork to the various butchers shops in town. In addition to this collection of carcases, sundry porkers are sinuggled into town under spotless sheets at the bottom of farmers' carts, and others come amongst a miscolkunsius assortment of agricultural produce, like oust saw last week, equalised in with a great heap of bumpers and further compressed by a load ot men and women, such as only a farmers' cart can carry. All these signs tend to show that the consumption of pork in Warrington inconsiderable, and as almost every reader is interested in this matter, task "Is pi,rk injurious ?" For my part, I answer the question in the affirmative, but with a view of interesting and elitiag the opinion of your readers, I give a report of a discussion that took place on this subject at a recent Family Council. The president mid that scarcely anything in the way of food came amiss to him, Kut Ito must confess to experiencing peculiar sensations after his lust feast on pork. The vice-president mid she hall no liking for pork, on the ground that it was "hard" eating, and it was very rarely that she touched it. Mr. A. remarked : You remember the two days I was ill recently ? Well, I did not say anything at the time, but that sickness was distinctly attributable to pork eating. I never reniember feeling so had before, but it was a lemon I've taken to heart, for I have now , eschewed pork altogether. Miss A. owned to being somewhat upmt after she last partook of the " unclean thing," but She was uncertain whether it was to be at down to the flesh of the pig, or to!tlie statement subsequently volunteered by the host that lie had been compellisl to kill the animal to merit from a natural death ! said pork did not agree" touched it.

" Hut ' -you efer w-ork-re'r again r " No ! " reeprmded the pnvident utnilingly. How. ever, my mate brought some ham and we ate it, but I , must say I was dreadfully had after it." " Well," mid Mr. J.," You should be like me, and eat , neither fish, flesh nor fowl. Then you mmld not suffer , half the ills you do. But I am surprised that, after marling the little pamphlet I lent you on the • perils of : pork,' you have touched the abominable thing again. However, you are paying for your experience ' in suffering, and I hope the result in your cages will be the same as in mine, I have told you what a festering mass of corruption a pig is, and what else can you expect from such an indiscriminate scavenger ? you know people thlnk anything goal enough to teed pigs on, and afterwards eat their flesh as a dainty. No wonder at folks being ill after eating fmrk."—Yours

A striking feature to the nn he approaches the works is the immense natramition which has been made for the entrance gates and leeks. From the cutting alone up to the end Dezember last, the 'quantity of earth, he., removed was 1,1130,000 cubit; yards. As far as excavating goes it is almost complete; only. small portion of the third or bottom lift now requires to be dug out. at which there are four steam navvim at work. The bottom width of the cutting is 380 feet, and the greatest breadth 440 feet, the latter varying acetwaling to the solidity of the sides. , The deepest part i 3 60 feet. In this cutting will be placed a series of three locks. One, 600 feet long by 80 firt wide ; a second, 350 feet long by 50 feet wide ; and a third 150 feet long by 30 feet 6 inches wide. Storm gates will be erected at both eals of the locks, which will bring the total length t,f the walls for the three hicks up to 750 feet wide, 506 feet respectively. Notwithststidieg ' the depth of the lock cutting, and its close proximity to the river, it is is far comparatively free from water. There are 1,300 men at present employed on this section, which number is being augmented every day. Every applicant for work, who could work. has been started sin, January Ist, and the agent expects to have at least 2,000 employed in a couple of months to coma.

The new store which is being erected here is almost built, and in a shirt time will be ready for one. At Thelwall the main work in hand at present is the river diversion, which was completed last week by the contractor on the Lynne side of the weir, known by the name of Butcher's Field. The spoil from the canal has beVII thrown across the river to ions the two banks of he Ship Canal, mid the lierince navvy last Saturday began the continuation of its work through the bed of the rive, working its way towards the ninth of the Benin. SUICIDE OF THE CROWN PRINCE.

The" Pill Mall Gazette " last evening publishes a state- ment, for the accuracy of which it vouches, to the effect that the Crown Prince Rudolphcommitted suicide, rather ths fights duel with the brother of a princess whom he had sed seed.
FRIDAY At-runt:now, VIRDNA.—The late Crown Prince bequeaths life interest in the whole of his property to his wife, and, at her death, the whole will go to his little daughter. OFFICIAL _REPORT..

VIENNA, FRIDA-lriii-I;...ofECCar::iiiener ?titling" to-day publishes the following statement concerning the cense of Crown Prince Rudolph's death : Professor Dr. Widerheder to Aleyerling, made an exam- ination and found in the head of the deceased a large wound, the pericranium and skull bones being partially shattered. This wound, whirls must have caused instant death, woo found to have been caused by a bullet, and by the side of the bed close to the Prince's right hand lay a revolver, one chamber of which had boon discharged. The position of the weapon left no doubt that the Prinee had met with his death by his own hand. As the Prince's servants wire lodged in adjoining houses, and as the Prince's personal attendant, having been directed by his Imperial Highness to mike arrangements for a shouting , excursion, had left the house bra short time, the report of the weapon could not litard by anyone. A COMMitt- sion was immediately despatched to Meverling with . instructions to draw up a protocol recordink the facts of . the case and the attendant circumstances. We cannot conceal the fact that several persons in the immediate' entourayt of the Prince perceived in Ws Imperial High- nees's manner during the past few weeks various indica- tions of morbid nervous excitement, a, that the view must be adhered to that tilk terrible event was the out- loam of temporary mental derangement. TUE POST-MORTEM EXAMINATION.

VIIENNA, FlllO., 9.45 A.id. The autopsy of the body of the Crown Prince was Commenced at nine p.m. Yesterday, in the presence of the heads of the Pathologi.ll Anatomical Institute, and a committee of high court officials. The post-mortem examination lasted until midnight. The remains were I removed in the course of the night to the great dining- ,: hall, where they were placed upon the bier. M. Tissa's audience of the Emperor was of the most affecting character. The Emperor took the Premier's hand in silence, and pressed it warmly. M. The funeral cortege will take the shortest route through the city to the Capuchins Church, in the vault of which the remains will be laid. Majority 224 MR, SPEAKMAN ON lITR VICTORY.

' Aft, the declaration of the poll. a number of Mr. Speakman's supporters gathered in bin Committee room, High-st., and the suceosaful candidatedelivenad a speech. Ile said he could not find words to give adespire wrote sion to his feelings. lie did fist think that any man in any constituency was ever blesaial with a more honest, hardworking or finer Committee than he had and it was to that Committee he owed his grand majority of 224 that night. (Cheers.) For the last 20 years it had been his lot to work in a ',Philo capacity in Runcorn, and he bid done no with an honest pitrpose and if he were spared. ha should go forth to the County Council pre- pared to do work there befitting the hnnoursthey had conferred upon hint that day. (Cheers.) Ile entered upon that contest with a single eye to do the thing that was right to his opponents and to hia constituents. Client, hear), and there was not one man on the opposite side that could say he hail ever said an unkind word to them. (Cheer.) The Liberal party (to which Annie people maid he did not helnng,hutthnt had been refuted) had gone through a crucial homing, hut the principle of Liberalism was strong and deep rented in Runcorn, and in future the position of the Liberal party would be maintained. (Cheers.) In that contest he had been largely supported by the Conservatives of the division ,applaumel and to them and to his friends the Liberals, he iaced Ida best thanks. In reinchision he proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Bridgewater. the Chairman of his Committee, and to Mr. Wynne Ilitniphreva, his agent. Mr. JAMPS KNMVl.l.4secondeil the motion, which was carried by acclamation. Mr. RONIPIERMYS acknnwletird thevotn in a few grace- ful sentenc,, and went on to nonark that Mr. Speakman owed a great deal of his majority to the ladies. and no one after thiA reuld deny that Mr. Speakman MRS a ladies' man. (Laughter.) If the onestion of women's suffrage came before the Comity Council and Mr. Speak- man had the temerity to vote against it he had better lookout for another constituency. (Laughter.) Ile was pleased to see in the room Mr. Wm. Handley who hail acted fir the ober candidate in the same capacity as he (Mr. Humphreys) had acted for Mr. )ipeakman— (hear, hear)—auil ha look his presence as an evidence that so far an the other side scar conrerned there was no bitter- ness oe ill-feeling in the matter at all. (applause.) They had fought honestly, and fairly and he hoped they might claim to have fought well, end as long as they were satisfied, he hoped Mr. Handley was satisfied. !Applause.)

As to the remarks Mr. Speakman had uttered, he did not think there , I was any occasion for bitterness lie knew those whom • he (Mr. Handley) represented felt neme-._rneac, hear and : pplansel —and he did not think the elertion would I•lateasgs the party to which they hoth belonged. ~tpplause.)
